title: One stop of light
subtitle: A small field guide to photographic exposure
creator: Palim
description: Understand what changes when you halve the light, then try it with your own camera.

chapters.title: Make one deliberate change
chapters.markdown:
A cyclist passes through a patch of evening light. You want the rider sharp, but your photograph is blurred. Making the whole image brighter will not solve that problem. You need a shorter exposure.

The useful question is simple: **what must stay still, and what can change?**

A camera gives you two physical ways to control the light reaching its sensor: the size of the lens opening and the time the shutter is open. ISO affects the brightness of the recorded image; it does not open the lens or keep the shutter open longer.

![An opening and an exposure time, compared](figure:light-path)

## Think in halves and doubles

A stop is a factor of two. Keeping the scene and aperture fixed, an exposure of 1/250 second admits twice as much light as 1/500 second. The shorter exposure gives a moving subject less time to travel across the frame.

That gives you a decision rather than a recipe: shorten the exposure to reduce motion blur, then decide how to compensate for the light you have given up.

chapters.title: Trade time for an opening
chapters.markdown:
Suppose your meter suggests **f/8 at 1/250 second, ISO 200**. You choose 1/500 second for the moving rider. That halves the exposure time. Opening the lens from f/8 to f/5.6 adds approximately one stop of light, compensating for the shorter time.

| Setting | Starting point | Faster shutter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Aperture | f/8 | f/5.6 |
| Shutter | 1/250 s | 1/500 s |
| ISO | 200 | 200 |

These are an illustrative pair of equivalent settings, not a prescription for every scene. The brightness can remain similar while the picture changes: the faster shutter reduces motion blur, and the wider opening can make less of the scene appear in focus.

![Relative light at three shutter times](figure:shutter-times)

## Keep the trade-off visible

If your lens cannot open further, increasing ISO may give a usable image brightness. It does not recover the light that never reached the sensor. The right compromise depends on the picture you are trying to make.

A sharp rider against a soft background may be exactly right. A landscape with detail from foreground to distance asks for a different choice.

chapters.title: Try three frames
chapters.markdown:
Choose a subject moving across your view: a person walking or leaves moving in the wind. Use a safe position and steady the camera. Keep the framing and available light as consistent as you can. Turn Auto ISO off and hold ISO at one value for all three frames; this lets you observe the aperture change without ISO changing as well.

1. In shutter-priority mode, make a frame at 1/125 second.
2. Make another at 1/250, then one at 1/500. Let the camera adjust the aperture; note if it reaches its limit.
3. Compare the moving edges at the same magnification. Look for a change in motion blur before judging overall brightness.

## Read the photograph, then the settings

Which frame expresses the movement you wanted? What did the camera change to make it? If the last frame is darker, did the lens run out of aperture?

Write down the answer in one sentence. That small observation is more useful than memorising a supposedly perfect setting.

**Take this with you:** choose the effect first. Change one setting deliberately. Notice what the camera has to trade in return.
